rationale: B wins because it has the same basic story instincts as A, but it keeps its hands cleaner. Its line "the user must supply names and dates — the fact block doesn't name them" is exactly the discipline A lacked before writing "Whoop Finally Has FDA-Cleared ECG. Apple Watch Has Had It for Years." A has one sharp keeper in "Whoop Calls Blood Pressure a 'Wellness Estimate.' That Word Choice Is Doing Legal Work," but it keeps decorating the supplied facts with competitor names and category assumptions. That is how a usable angle turns into a fact-check problem.
gaps_in_A: "Whoop Finally Has FDA-Cleared ECG. Apple Watch Has Had It for Years." Apple is not in the supplied facts. The update only says competitors already ship FDA-cleared ECG; naming Apple turns a defensible counterposition into an unsupported claim.

"Apple Watch includes ECG with hardware, no subscription gate — confirm this" is a proof item masquerading as a fact. If it needs confirmation, it does not belong as the spine of the access angle yet.

"The wearable industry has spent years positioning cuffless blood pressure monitoring as the next frontier" is an outside trend claim with no evidence in the update. It may be true, but this set was supposed to stay grounded.
"The $3.6 Billion Wearable That Still Needs a Blood Pressure Cuff" slightly overplays the friction. The fact says one-time cuff calibration, not ongoing cuff dependency.
gaps_in_B: "catch-up-and-leapfrog story" overreaches. Whoop may be catching up on ECG, but a non-medical BP wellness estimate requiring cuff calibration is not yet a leapfrog without proof.
"the average wearer can't tell the difference" is plausible, but unsupported. Good regulatory angle, lazy reader claim.
"Cuffless blood pressure is the next wearable battleground" is a broad category thesis that needs market evidence. The update supports a Whoop launch, not the whole battleground.
The regulatory angle should explicitly ask whether Whoop submitted the blood-pressure feature to FDA at all. "Why BP shipped as wellness" is close, but not sharp enough for the key regulatory fact.
